item.title: I replaced $180-a-year software subscription with my web-browser, and I wish I'd done it sooner
item.itunes:title: I replaced $180-a-year software subscription with my web-browser, and I wish I'd done it sooner
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I used to treat Adobe Acrobat as one of those apps you simply needed if you worked with PDFs regularly. Whenever I came across a PDF-related task, my first thought was usually to find a dedicated tool that could handle it. Over time, though, I started questioning whether I was making things more complicated than they needed to be. Microsoft Edge had been sitting on my computer all along, and I hadn't really paid attention to what it could do with PDFs. Once I started using it more seriously, I realized I had been overlooking a useful part of a browser I already used every day.

Edge became my default PDF viewer

PDFs found a new home

I didn't plan to make Microsoft Edge my PDF viewer. It happened simply because I was already using Edge for most of my work. Whenever a PDF landed in my inbox, or I downloaded one while researching an article, I started opening it there instead of sending it to another application.

That small change made my workflow feel much simpler. I don't have to think about which program I should use before opening a document. I click the PDF, and it loads in the same browser I already have open. I also like how quickly I can get into a document. If I'm checking a report, reading documentation, or looking through a PDF for something specific, Edge gets me there without making the task feel like a separate part of my workflow.

After doing this repeatedly, opening PDFs in Edge just became my default. I stopped associating PDFs with a dedicated desktop application. For the kind of documents I handle during a normal blogging day, the browser is now the obvious starting point.

The built-in PDF tools cover my everyday needs

The basics are more than enough

What made me keep using Edge was its simple PDF tools. They cover most of the things I need to do with a PDF. I usually don't need to make big changes to a document. Most of the time, I just need to read it, find something, highlight it, or add a quick note.

The search tool is one of the features I use the most. When I'm working with a long PDF, I don't have to go through every page to find a word or sentence. I can search for it and jump straight to the right place. This is helpful when I'm using reports or documents for research.

I also use the annotation tools when I'm reviewing something. I can highlight text, draw on the page, or add a note when I want to remember something. If I find a useful point while reading, I can mark it and keep going instead of writing everything down separately.

These tools are simple, but that's what I like about them. They handle the PDF tasks I normally need without making things harder than they need to be. For my regular work, that's more than enough.

5 free PDF editors that make Adobe Acrobat feel outdated

Why pay for Acrobat when these free PDF editors can handle it all?

15
By  Nolen Jonker

PDF workflow stays inside the browser

No need to manage two separate apps

Another thing I like about Edge is that I don't need a separate app just for PDFs. I can handle the documents I work with without adding another program to my setup. That also means fewer things to install and maintain. I don't have to search for a PDF reader, keep another app updated, or worry about whether I have the right software for a basic document.

I prefer keeping my setup simple, especially when I'm working for long hours. Every extra application adds a little more clutter, even if I only use it occasionally. For me, a PDF reader doesn't need to be something I think about. I just want to open a document and get on with my work. Edge fits that approach well. It may not sound like a major change, but removing one unnecessary app from my workflow makes things feel a little easier. I don't need to build a separate PDF setup when the tools I already use are enough for my everyday work.

Edge isn't replacing Acrobat

Not built for everything

I don't see Edge as a complete replacement for Adobe Acrobat, and I don't think it needs to be. There are still times when I'd want dedicated PDF software. If I need to make major changes to a document, create PDFs, or handle more advanced PDF work, a proper PDF application makes more sense.

But those aren't the things I usually need to do. Most of my PDF work is fairly simple, so keeping a full Acrobat-style app around doesn't feel necessary. That's really what changed for me. I wasn't looking for an app that could copy everything Acrobat does. I just needed something that could handle the PDF tasks I actually deal with. Edge does that well enough for my needs. So I'm not calling it an Acrobat replacement. I simply stopped searching for one.

4 open‑source PDF tools that replace Adobe Acrobat for everyday work

PDF power without the monthly subscription

3
By  Yash Patel

Sometimes, the best alternative is already on your PC

I don't think I'll ever stop needing different tools for different jobs. But this experience changed how I look for them. Now, before downloading another app, I first check whether something I already use can handle the job. In this case, Microsoft Edge was more capable than I had given it credit for. It saved me from adding another piece of software to my setup, and sometimes, that simple solution is all I need.

item.title: OpenAI weighs hitting the brakes on AI, hoping rivals accept a ceasefire they might just ignore
item.itunes:title: OpenAI weighs hitting the brakes on AI, hoping rivals accept a ceasefire they might just ignore
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • OpenAI may pause AI development to contain powerful LLM risks, urging rivals to follow.
  • Top researchers call for voluntary slowdowns and shared safety standards amid misuse fears.
  • But other firms or overseas players may ignore a pause, risking a global AI race and leapfrogging.

In a race, it's always risky to stop to take a breather and hope that your opponents will do the same, especially if you're the one to beat. OpenAI seems to believe it has a shot, as it's currently mulling over putting the brakes on AI advancement for now, with the hope that the rivals snapping at its heels will also opt to take a rest.

OpenAI wants an AI race time-out, and it wants its competitors to respect it

Will anyone actually do that, though?

As reported by Bloomberg, Sam Altman held a company-wide meeting to discuss what's next with the AI company. It's getting to the point where AI models are so powerful that they can launch cyberattacks on other websites and services, which has caused some concern about how quickly LLMs are progressing without proper safeguards.

As such, Altman said that OpenAI is ready and willing to put AI advancement on the back burner while it figures out how to contain this new power its AI models have. He hopes that other AI companies will follow suit instead of taking the opportunity to leapfrog over AI, but he's seemingly aware that some firms will refuse to play ball.

In fact, OpenAI's top scientist, Jakub Pachocki, hopes AI companies can put down their weapons by “coordinating to slow down future development as needed." He's personally hoping "for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.”

So, what are the odds that other AI companies will respect the need to slow down? Well, Claude's Anthropic seems to be experiencing a similar scare, after one of its safety engineers stated that they believed AI has over a 10% chance of ending the human race. However, even if OpenAI can convince all of the US-based LLM firms to link arms together, it does open the door for overseas businesses to overtake them all in a move reminiscent of DeepSeek's big AI shake-up.

Linus Torvalds used AI to fix a Linux bug, and now LLM critics on Linux face an uncomfortable choice

Avoiding software without AI code is getting very difficult.

By  Simon Batt

item.title: I stopped letting Windows decide where my files go, and my SSD stopped filling up
item.itunes:title: I stopped letting Windows decide where my files go, and my SSD stopped filling up
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Over the past few months, I've uncovered how the default settings Windows 11 decides are usually not in the best interest of users, whether it's about user experience, accessibility, resource allocation, or even power plans. Most of these are very obviously tuned in a way that's not optimal for most users, and for those with multiple drives, this aspect applies to storage as well.

The past few weeks have got me rethinking how I manage my PC's combined 1.2 terabytes of storage, which pinches just past the 1TB mark most users work with in 2026, but a little lower than optimal capacity on a dedicated workstation. This is exactly why reclaiming control over my storage from Windows' grasp became so important, especially since its defaults insisted everything belonged on the boot drive.

OneDrive was turning my second drive into a spectator

Moving the sync folder can reclaim a decent chunk of space

The first thing I looked at was OneDrive, primarily because it was creating a rather paradoxical situation on my PC with a PCIe Gen 4 NVMe and a SATA SSD. I had a perfectly good second storage solution sitting mostly unoccupied, while Microsoft's cloud storage was ballooning up in my boot drive, because I like to keep the files always on the device.

If you use OneDrive, its local folder naturally gets assigned a spot on your boot drive. That can become expensive once you start keeping portions of cloud library available offline. Worse still, if you've enabled OneDrive's backup for Desktop, Documents, or Pictures, those Windows folders can become a part of the OneDrive ecosystem as well.

Fortunately, there is an option to move OneDrive itself rather than struggle with individual folders. From OneDrive's settings, you can unlink the PC. Before signing back in, manually move the existing OneDrive folder to the secondary drive so that when you select that folder during setup, OneDrive can index and merge local files instead of re-downloading everything. OneDrive will then proceed to sync against that location instead of ballooning up on the boot drive.

This is the one Windows setting I always change first on any PC

OneDrive sync wastes bandwidth and storage, so it's one of the first settings I turn off.

11
By  Brian Burgess

Clearing this space is pointless if it keeps refilling

That's why my new files needed a new destination

If I simply just moved the bulk of my C: drive to the D: drive, it'd quickly become a repetitive chore that I'd have to go through month after month, or week after week to save my Crucial T500 from the constant write cycles that Windows puts it through. As such, I needed to stop the leak before I bothered to mop the floor.

What most people don't know is that there's a simple fix to this exact predicament that Windows makes available through the settings, and to Microsoft's credit, the option is quite accessible. All you have to do to find it is go to Settings, then System, followed by Storage, then go into Advanced Storage Settings below it. This will unveil an option that most users will not have seen before, which is "Where new content is saved".

The dropdowns here on this menu allow you to specify the destination for new file downloads. I could just change the dropdowns to D:, which gives the system a place to put new content instead of continually adding to the drive that would fill itself to critical levels over a period of a few months. Embarrassingly enough, even I discovered it by going through a couple of posts on Microsoft Tech Community forums.

I make this one change to make Windows faster

One simple toggle can speed up your Windows experience

15
By  Ty Sherback

One file refused to leave C:, so I got rid of it instead

hiberfil.sys has to be on the boot drive, but my desktop doesn't need it at all

Most of the storage strain Windows was putting on my boot drive could simply be migrated elsewhere, but then I found one particularly stubborn exception by the name of hiberfil.sys. If you've been following my coverage, you'd know that I stumbled upon the 12.5-gigabyte file while going through my NVMe SSD and found that the reason it exists is because of a Windows feature called Fast Startup.

The file sits on your C: drive, holding the contents of your system memory, and it does so to hold the contents of RAM, which allows the machine to hibernate. Unlike the page file, it must always stay on the boot drive, and there's no supported way to move it to another.

How big the file gets depends on your system memory, because it can grow up to 40% of its size. On my machine with 32GB of DDR5 memory, it grew up to 12.5GB, which is exactly 39%. I'd argue that hibernation is a useful feature on mobile devices like laptops where there's actually a use case for preserving a session and resuming later, but on a desktop backed by a PCIe Gen 4 SSD that can be up and running in no time, the extra storage matters more.

To make the hiberfil.sys file go away, you too, can use the following command on an elevated CMD or PowerShell. Bear in mind, this also does away with Fast Startup functionality. 

powercfg /hibernate off 

The boot drive doesn't have to be the default location for everything

It's widely acknowledged that Windows defaults don't really serve the users all that well, and the same logic applies to how storage is managed on the drives as well. However, it's also true that the OS is flexible enough for the savvy user to take back control, redirect (or eliminate) the biggest offenders and manage their storage better themselves.

item.content:encoded:
Over the past few months, I've uncovered how the default settings Windows 11 decides are usually not in the best interest of users, whether it's about user experience, accessibility, resource allocation, or even power plans. Most of these are very obviously tuned in a way that's not optimal for most users, and for those with multiple drives, this aspect applies to storage as well.

The past few weeks have got me rethinking how I manage my PC's combined 1.2 terabytes of storage, which pinches just past the 1TB mark most users work with in 2026, but a little lower than optimal capacity on a dedicated workstation. This is exactly why reclaiming control over my storage from Windows' grasp became so important, especially since its defaults insisted everything belonged on the boot drive.

OneDrive was turning my second drive into a spectator

Moving the sync folder can reclaim a decent chunk of space

The first thing I looked at was OneDrive, primarily because it was creating a rather paradoxical situation on my PC with a PCIe Gen 4 NVMe and a SATA SSD. I had a perfectly good second storage solution sitting mostly unoccupied, while Microsoft's cloud storage was ballooning up in my boot drive, because I like to keep the files always on the device.

If you use OneDrive, its local folder naturally gets assigned a spot on your boot drive. That can become expensive once you start keeping portions of cloud library available offline. Worse still, if you've enabled OneDrive's backup for Desktop, Documents, or Pictures, those Windows folders can become a part of the OneDrive ecosystem as well.

Fortunately, there is an option to move OneDrive itself rather than struggle with individual folders. From OneDrive's settings, you can unlink the PC. Before signing back in, manually move the existing OneDrive folder to the secondary drive so that when you select that folder during setup, OneDrive can index and merge local files instead of re-downloading everything. OneDrive will then proceed to sync against that location instead of ballooning up on the boot drive.

This is the one Windows setting I always change first on any PC

OneDrive sync wastes bandwidth and storage, so it's one of the first settings I turn off.

11
By  Brian Burgess

Clearing this space is pointless if it keeps refilling

That's why my new files needed a new destination

If I simply just moved the bulk of my C: drive to the D: drive, it'd quickly become a repetitive chore that I'd have to go through month after month, or week after week to save my Crucial T500 from the constant write cycles that Windows puts it through. As such, I needed to stop the leak before I bothered to mop the floor.

What most people don't know is that there's a simple fix to this exact predicament that Windows makes available through the settings, and to Microsoft's credit, the option is quite accessible. All you have to do to find it is go to Settings, then System, followed by Storage, then go into Advanced Storage Settings below it. This will unveil an option that most users will not have seen before, which is "Where new content is saved".

The dropdowns here on this menu allow you to specify the destination for new file downloads. I could just change the dropdowns to D:, which gives the system a place to put new content instead of continually adding to the drive that would fill itself to critical levels over a period of a few months. Embarrassingly enough, even I discovered it by going through a couple of posts on Microsoft Tech Community forums.

I make this one change to make Windows faster

One simple toggle can speed up your Windows experience

15
By  Ty Sherback

One file refused to leave C:, so I got rid of it instead

hiberfil.sys has to be on the boot drive, but my desktop doesn't need it at all

Most of the storage strain Windows was putting on my boot drive could simply be migrated elsewhere, but then I found one particularly stubborn exception by the name of hiberfil.sys. If you've been following my coverage, you'd know that I stumbled upon the 12.5-gigabyte file while going through my NVMe SSD and found that the reason it exists is because of a Windows feature called Fast Startup.

The file sits on your C: drive, holding the contents of your system memory, and it does so to hold the contents of RAM, which allows the machine to hibernate. Unlike the page file, it must always stay on the boot drive, and there's no supported way to move it to another.

How big the file gets depends on your system memory, because it can grow up to 40% of its size. On my machine with 32GB of DDR5 memory, it grew up to 12.5GB, which is exactly 39%. I'd argue that hibernation is a useful feature on mobile devices like laptops where there's actually a use case for preserving a session and resuming later, but on a desktop backed by a PCIe Gen 4 SSD that can be up and running in no time, the extra storage matters more.

To make the hiberfil.sys file go away, you too, can use the following command on an elevated CMD or PowerShell. Bear in mind, this also does away with Fast Startup functionality. 

powercfg /hibernate off 

The boot drive doesn't have to be the default location for everything

It's widely acknowledged that Windows defaults don't really serve the users all that well, and the same logic applies to how storage is managed on the drives as well. However, it's also true that the OS is flexible enough for the savvy user to take back control, redirect (or eliminate) the biggest offenders and manage their storage better themselves.

item.title: Claude in Chrome is the best debugging tool I could ever ask for
item.itunes:title: Claude in Chrome is the best debugging tool I could ever ask for
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Claude Code has already made our lives so much easier. But with the more recent announcement of Claude in Chrome, the tool has now become an absolute go-to for development. I'm saying this because, before this, if you were designing something or trying to point out a design bug, a front-end bug, or pretty much any issue with the UI, you had a couple of options. You could ask Claude to inspect the code and try to figure out what was wrong from there, or you could share screenshots of the issues you were seeing and explain what needed to be fixed.

And if you needed to do this repeatedly, you could set up some kind of automation using Playwright, where you'd have a routine that opens the application, takes screenshots, and verifies different states of the UI. But all in all, this process has always been pretty cumbersome. With Claude in Chrome, you can basically allow Claude to visit the same front-end you're looking at, inspect what is actually happening in the browser, figure out what is wrong, make the necessary changes in the code, and then come back and verify whether the fix worked.

Claude in Chrome is a game changer for debugging

Claude can now actually see what's wrong

Earlier, your flow would usually be that Claude Code writes the application, you run it in Chrome, and Claude understands what is happening primarily through the code itself. If you're able to see that something is misaligned or visually off, you then have to explain it to Claude or paste a screenshot.

For example, there have been many times when I've asked Claude to build something, maybe a landing page or the UI for a feature, and technically it builds what I asked for, but something just looks wrong. Sometimes a button isn't centered, the spacing is off, or the text gets truncated. Sometimes an element overflows its container or a layout looks fine on one screen size but completely breaks on another. With Claude in Chrome, you can simply ask Claude to take a look at the application itself and work out what needs to be fixed.

And it goes far beyond design issues. Claude can inspect console errors, network activity, and the DOM state. It can navigate through your application, click buttons, fill in forms, move through different screens, and observe what happens after each interaction.

Let's say you've built a login flow and clicking the login button doesn't do anything. Earlier, Claude would inspect the authentication code and try to reason about where the problem could be. Now it can actually open the application, fill in the form, click the login button, see whether an error appears in the console, inspect whether the API request failed, check what the browser did afterward, trace that problem back to the code, fix it, reload the application, and test the whole flow again.

Your CLAUDE.md is probably wrong, and here's how Anthropic's engineers actually structure theirs

Your file is probably doing more harm than good

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

It also works really well for design verification

You can use it to replicate a design

Claude in Chrome isn't just useful for debugging. It also works really well when you want to replicate a design. For example, if you want Claude to build a landing page similar to those of your competitors, you can ask it to go through their actual websites. You could even have it analyze multiple competitors and then implement what each of them does best. As I mentioned above, you can keep asking Claude to visually verify the design until it gets it right. The only caveat is that Claude in Chrome consumes a lot of your usage allowance, so verifying something multiple times can eat through your usage limit very quickly.

Of course, Claude in Chrome doesn't make tools like Playwright unnecessary. For deterministic regression testing, where you want the same tests to run automatically every time you push code, Playwright still makes a lot of sense.

Claude in Chrome works with logged-in apps

My personal favorite feature

My favorite feature, though, is probably the fact that Claude in Chrome works with the accounts you're already logged into. A lot of the apps you actually need to test are dashboards, admin panels, internal tools, staging environments, and CRMs, which aren't publicly accessible. And getting an agent into those environments otherwise is a huge pain.

You either need to give it access through an API, set up some integration, figure out authentication for your browser automation, or deal with sessions, cookies, SSO, and sometimes MFA.

Claude in Chrome basically skips that problem because it works inside your existing browser session. If you're already logged into the application, Claude can work with the page in front of you using that same login. Anthropic specifically calls out internal tools, legacy portals, admin consoles, and other systems without APIs as use cases for this. So you can open your app, log in normally, and then tell Claude to go reproduce the issue.

ChatGPT also has the same feature

If you are not using Claude, which I understand because the usage limits are insane, ChatGPT also offers the same feature through its browser extension. It works in a similar way, but you get better usage limits.

Claude Code's creator keeps sharing tips, and they all made my experience better

Who better to learn from than the person who built it?

item.title: I gave Sunshine a virtual display, and game streams stopped hijacking my monitor
item.itunes:title: I gave Sunshine a virtual display, and game streams stopped hijacking my monitor
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The idea of streaming my own video game library on a different device in the house, without being tied to the physical desk-and-chair setup, is hard to resist. That's why I jumped down the game-hosting rabbit hole with the universal first step — Sunshine. I expected a simple setup and a few tweaks before I could get gaming and forget about the hosting software, but I was wrong.

When I connected to any other device on my local network — my 4K TV, my 1080p laptop, or even my iPhone — I watched my PC's physical monitor mirror the client-side device. The display changed, the desktop shifted, and what was supposed to be a "remote" gaming session became all too visible on my primary monitor. The biggest problem, of course, was that my physical monitor mirrored my stream, which was supposed to happen off the computer.

I didn't want to buy a dummy HDMI plug to cleanly separate the two screens, though. Since Sunshine only needs a display, I gave it one that doesn't physically exist.

Sunshine worked perfectly until I connected to it

My physical monitor kept becoming part of the stream

I began where everyone does — I installed Sunshine from scratch, left its settings at their defaults, and installed Moonlight on my 1080p 60Hz laptop. This laptop doesn't have a discrete GPU or a beefy CPU, but it doesn't need them either, since it only has to decode the game's video stream from my PC. On my laptop, I expected Moonlight to simply receive a 1080p60fps stream, but the moment I started the desktop stream, my physical monitor began mirroring the stream as well. My browser tabs, word processors, and messenger apps, all disappeared because the stream was displaying only Steam's Big Picture Mode.

I wrongly assumed it was an oddity with the laptop, but it became evident pretty quickly that my supposedly remote display was dictating what the screen on my desk should do, rearranging its resolution, scale, and refresh rate, and, consequently, my entire desktop icon arrangement as well.

Soon enough, this behavior made sense once I understood what Sunshine was capturing. With a normal installation, it works with the display Windows exposes. Sunshine works with the display Windows exposes to it and streams that display to Moonlight. The client gets a video feed of the desktop, but only one screen is involved — the physical monitor on my desk.

I realized I had approached Sunshine with the wrong assumption. I didn't need the stream to control or mirror my physical display; I needed Sunshine to have its own display. The obvious question was how to give it one without buying another monitor.

5 self-hosted apps that replaced my expensive paid subscriptions without feeling like a downgrade

So much money saved for barely any compromises

By  Samarveer Singh

I stopped fighting Sunshine and gave it another display

I had to stop it from using my monitor

My first instinct was to try the obvious fix: make Sunshine match the client. I enabled resolution matching, expecting the 1080p laptop to stop making things strange. It did exactly what I asked, but that made the problem more obvious. Sadly, my monitor dropped to 1080p60Hz, and the stream was still using the physical screen.

That was the wrong rabbit hole, though. The issue wasn't that Sunshine was changing my resolution. The stream was being rendered on the monitor on my desk. No amount of resolution switching could change that, so I needed to move the stream somewhere my physical display couldn't see.

That's where a virtual display driver comes in. It creates a headless monitor in software for Sunshine to capture. I didn't want to buy a dummy HDMI plug, but this let me use that plug without a physical one. Windows believes another screen is connected, but nothing physical has to change. I headed over to Virtual Display Driver's GitHub page, downloaded the VDC app, and installed a virtual display at 1080p60Hz. Next, I restarted Sunshine so the virtual display's ID would appear in Sunshine's boot logs.

You can identify and copy the virtual "MTT by VDD" display's GUID, by opening Sunshine.log via Notepad. It's located in C: > Program Files > Sunshine > Config.

With the Display ID secured, I opened up Sunshine's Web UI in my local browser (usually localhost:47990), and went to Configuration > Audio/Video > Display ID. There, I pasted the Display ID for the VDC virtual display, then clicked Advanced Display Device options to ensure Device Configuration was set to "Activate the display automatically and make it a primary display."

With that done, Sunshine streams the virtual display I added, and that's the stream my laptop or TV picks up now, leaving my monitor free.

My old phone plays my PC games better than the latest flagships ever could, thanks to this free app

My PC games don't exist exclusively on my desk anymore

7
By  Samarveer Singh

The virtual display proved useful beyond fixing the problem

Three reasons I'm keeping it around

With Sunshine properly configured now, I finally have my primary monitor free while the stream runs straight to my laptop or TV. The obvious benefit is that my partner can game while I'm away from the desk. If I'm making coffee, stuck in a meeting, or finished for the night, she can pick up the laptop and play a game without taking over my monitor. I don't have to log out, hand over my keyboard, or set up my desktop for her.

It also makes sharing the PC less ridiculous. I can keep watching a movie on my monitor while my partner games on the laptop, which is useful when buying another gaming PC currently requires the sort of financial planning I'd otherwise reserve for buying a car. Each session has its own display, so neither interferes.

When I'm streaming, the separation means I can keep using the desktop. A game can occupy the virtual screen while my browser or messaging apps remain on the physical monitor. Sunshine finally behaves like a streaming tool rather than a remote button.

Sunshine
See at Github
The NVIDIA App's Game Optimizer is genuinely magic, and it's not appreciated enough

So many hours I've saved in an increasingly busy life

19
By  Samarveer Singh

My monitor finally gets to stay out of the conversation

It's been oddly satisfying to solve a problem that initially feels like it should require more hardware. I didn't need another gaming PC, another monitor, or another increasingly elaborate collection of cables dangling behind my desk. On my laptop, I expected Moonlight to simply receive a 1080p60fps stream, but the moment I started the desktop stream, my physical monitor began mirroring the stream as well. My browser tabs, word processors, and messenger apps, all disappeared because the stream was displaying only Steam's Big Picture Mode.

item.title: The 3 tiny Docker containers that turned a cheap server into my private cloud
item.itunes:title: The 3 tiny Docker containers that turned a cheap server into my private cloud
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I used to think building a private cloud meant installing something massive like Nextcloud, configuring a dozen services, and turning a cheap server into another full-time project. I was wrong.

I only needed three small Docker containers to cover most of what I actually wanted from the cloud: keeping my files in sync, storing my documentation and notes, and managing my passwords.

The setup is lightweight, easy to maintain, and runs well on modest software.

9 Docker containers that run 24/7 on my $100 mini PC

Maximum value budget homelab.

18
By  Samir Makwana

Syncthing

The quiet backbone of my cloud

Syncthing is the container that makes this entire private-cloud setup click for me. I have files across my Windows desktop, laptops, phone, and server, and I don’t want to manually copy them around every time I make a change. With Syncthing, I can pick the folders I care about, connect my devices, and let it handle the rest in the background.

That simplicity is what I like most about it. I can have a work folder on my Windows PC automatically synchronized with my server, for example. If I add a document, edit an article draft, rename a folder, or delete something, Syncthing can replicate those changes to the other connected devices.

In another example, I use Syncthing to sync my Pixel 8 screenshots folder to my Mac. That way, my screenshots are already there on my MacBook Pro, and I can easily upload them to my drafts.

Syncthing also gives me much more control over how each folder behaves. The standard Send & Receive mode works exactly as I would expect, but I can also create Send Only or Receive Only folders. That is useful when I want my server to act more like a destination rather than another machine where I edit files.

Syncthing has a web interface where I can see my folders, connected devices, sync status, transfer activity, and whether anything is out of sync. For me, that is why Syncthing is such a crucial part of this setup. Docmost and Vaultwarden add specific services to my private cloud, but Syncthing handles the thing I need constantly: making sure my important files are where I need them.

Once that happens automatically in the background, my cheap server starts feeling like infrastructure I can depend on every day.

Docmost

Where all my knowledge now lives

I use Docmost as my private documentation hub where I can store project notes, setup guides, ideas, reference material, and anything else that matters in my work and homelab.

The interface is one of the main reasons I like it. Docmost feels much closer to a modern workspace like Notion than an old-school wiki. I can create different spaces for separate areas of my life and work, nest pages underneath them, add tables, code blocks, attachments, comments, and organize everything without making the structure complicated.

The built-in diagram tools are another big plus for me. Docmost supports Draw.io, Excalidraw, and Mermaid, so I can create flowcharts, network diagrams, or quick visual explanations directly alongside my documentation.

Docmost also supports Bases that add Kanban boards and complex databases to the documents. However, it’s limited to paid plans only.

Most importantly, the whole thing runs on my own server. Syncthing gives me control over my files, while Docmost gives all that information structure and context.

5 open-source apps that are so good their premium versions are worth paying for

Not paywalled, just worth paying for.

32
By  Yash Patel

Vaultwarden

The smallest container guards everything

Vaultwarden is probably the most sensitive container in this entire setup because it stores the keys to almost everything else I use. Instead of relying on third-party password vaults like 1Password or LastPass, I can keep my passwords, logins, secure notes, and other credentials on my own server while still using the familiar Bitwarden ecosystem.

I don’t have to give up the convenience of browser extensions, mobile apps, desktop clients, or the web vault just because I want to self-host. Vaultwarden is compatible with Bitwarden clients, so that experience still feels polished and familiar.

I can save new logins, generate storage passwords, organize credentials, and access them from the devices I use every day.

I also like how lightweight the whole setup is. I don’t need to deploy a huge identity-management stack just to host my password vault. Of course, self-hosting passwords is one area where I can’t take shortcuts.

I keep Vaultwarden updated, use HTTPS, protect the account with strong authentication, and treat backups as mandatory. It may be a tiny container, but in terms of importance, it is easily one of the biggest services running on my server.

No subscriptions, no storage limits

I don’t think a private cloud needs to start with a giant server, a complicated dashboard, or ten containers running at once. Syncthing, Docmost, and Vaultwarden cover a huge part of what I expect from a personal cloud.

Immich is next on my list because moving away from Google Photos will be the hardest part of this entire transition. If you are thinking about building your own private cloud, start small.

Pick two or three services you will genuinely use, get comfortable with them, and expand only when you actually need more.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
There's certainly no shortage of network mapping and monitoring tools. There is one lightweight package I recently discovered and finally got around to testing. LAN Orangutan (what a name) quickly became one of my favorite snappy Docker containers to have running within the home lab. It has bags of potential with an early release that already gets almost everything right. It's quick to deploy, keeps things simple, and provides an effective way to map out and monitor networks.

When network scanners are useful at home

It's not just a tool for enthusiasts

Network scanning isn't something reserved for those who enjoy looking at numbers, discovered entities, and who enjoy having live views of what's happening on the LAN. It's also valuable for everyone else who may be interacting with clients and destinations on the network. Most devices on a typical home LAN receive an IP address from the router's DHCP server. A few IP addresses to remember is no big deal.

But once you start self-hosting services and appliacations, get more hardware online, and even venture into smart home territory, the LAN can quickly grow to three digits. That's when things become overbearing to recall every address on the network. Spinning up a new Linux container (LXC) or virtual machine (VM)? That'll be another IP address to remember. Want to use a VLAN for dedicated traffic segmentation and management? More IP addresses, please.

It does exactly what it says on GitHub.

This is where a network discovery tool such as LAN Orangutan comes into play. I've used a few over the years, including NetBox, Fing, Nmap, and Angry IP Scanner. They're all brilliant, but LAN Orangutan caught my eye as it's self-hosted, simple, and lightweight. In fact, it doesn't really do much aside from probe the network and list all clients. Sure, this data is likely available within the router software I use, but it looks much better and is more convenient to access.

Plus, it allows me to provide access to others, as I wouldn't want just about anyone accessing the router backend, right?

I used this self-hosted tool to scan my network, and it's surprisingly powerful

Reconya gives you real-time visibility into every device on your network.

8
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Setting up LAN Orangutan is easy

Up and running in less than a couple of minutes

Credit: 

The LAN scanner is available via Docker, which makes the entire process of launching and maintaining LAN Orangutan a painless process, even if this just so happens to be your first time running a Docker container. If you're using a GUI solution such as Portainer to manage self-hosted apps, you can simply install LAN Orangutan via the interface and you're good to go. If, like me, you prefer to run an LXC per app, here's how it's done:

  1. Create a Debian LXC.
  2. Enter the LXC shell.
  3. Update the system. apt update && apt upgrade -y
  4. Install Docker, certificate backend, and cURL. apt install docker ca-certificates curl
  5. Create the APT keyring directory. install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
  6. Add Docker's GPG key. curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/debian/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
  7. Adjust permissions on the Docker keyring file. chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
  8. Add the Docker repository. 
    tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources Types: deb
    URIs: https://download.docker.com/linux/debian
    Suites: $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME")
    Components: stable
    Architectures: $(dpkg --print-architecture)
    Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
    EOF

item.title: Google Dreambeans is now available to all US users; yes, even free tiers
item.itunes:title: Google Dreambeans is now available to all US users; yes, even free tiers
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Dreambeans is now open to all US users (18+), no subscription required.
  • It runs while you sleep to deliver a morning digest from Calendar, Gmail, Photos, Search, YouTube, and Gemini.
  • Available on Android and iOS, but limited to US residents aged 18+.

A little while ago, Google introduced a new AI tool called Dreambeans. It's an experimental AI tool that helps you start the day right by generating a personalised digest about your interests. At the time, you had to be part of a paid subscriber and join a waitlist to use it, but now the company has opened its doors to everyone in the US; yes, even free users.

Google Dreambeans is now available regardless of your subscription tier

It's still tied to the US, and you need to be 18+

As announced on the Google Labs blog, the company has announced the general rollout for Dreambeans. It was previously a paid-exclusive experiment back in June, but it has apparently done so well that Google is ready to bring this to all users, regardless of their subscription tier (if any).

If you've never heard of it, Google Dreambeans works away while you're not using your phone; for instance, while you're asleep. It checks all of your interests and data for anything interesting, then gives it to you when you wake up as a quick digest of everything that's happening. That's why it's called Dreambeans; the 'Dream' part references how it does everything while you sleep, while the 'Beans' half represents serving you a hot mug of information coffee to get yourself started every day.

Here's what Google Dreambeans uses to gather its data:

  • Personalized topics: This could be everything from places to explore, shows to watch, or a reminder of upcoming events.
  • Connected apps: Distilled information from the Google apps you select, including Calendar, Gmail, Photos, Search, YouTube, and now Gemini.

If you're interested, head over to the Dreambeans download page and grab it for Android or iOS. You need to be a US resident and 18+ to partake in Dreambeans.

I use ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Gemini daily — here's the only one worth paying for

One stands above the rest.

16
By  Mahnoor Faisal

item.title: I cloned an old SSD to save time, but it created more problems than it solved
item.itunes:title: I cloned an old SSD to save time, but it created more problems than it solved
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Four years ago, I had a choice in front of me: a clean Windows install on my new SSD or clone my old SSD. I had just set up my new gaming PC, and wanted to replace my old SATA SSD with the new Gen4 NVMe drive. I knew cloning the old SSD would be simple enough with Macrium Reflect, and I could pick up exactly where I left off. So, that's what I picked.

The problems started a few months down the line when my Windows installation started experiencing frequent corruption. The myriad of Windows issues that I couldn't solve should have prompted me to reinstall the OS, but I remained oblivious. I realized it too late that my old Windows 10 installation was riddled with too many underlying issues, and cloning my SSD gave those issues a new life on my new PC.

Here's what's on my "break in case of emergency" spare SSD

My spare SSD with Windows 11 is ready to go in case of a boot failure

9
By  Tanveer Singh

I couldn't be bothered to install Windows from scratch

I wanted to jump into my new system ASAP

Back in 2022, I moved from my older Ryzen 5 1600 and GTX 1660 Ti build to a Ryzen 7 5700X and RTX 3080 system. Until then, my old SATA SSD, a Samsung 860 EVO, had remained my boot drive for about four years. I had never used an NVMe SSD as the primary drive, and was finally excited to move everything to the WD Black SN770, a decent Gen4 NVMe SSD.

I had known about cloning drives and partitions for a while, but that was the first time I had the opportunity to do it. So, I installed Macrium Reflect and cloned my SATA SSD to the new Gen4 SSD. It saved me the hassle of installing a fresh copy of Windows and setting it up just the way I liked. The cloning process allowed me to continue using the Windows 10 environment that I was used to for years.

At first, I didn't notice anything to indicate that cloning my OS partition was a bad decision. Everything worked as intended, and the performance wasn't an issue either. It was only after a few months that the cracks began to show.

5 things to consider when upgrading to a larger SSD

Upgrading to a larger SSD comes with several important considerations, especially if you want to use it as the boot drive

By  Tanveer Singh

The old Windows installation brought its problems along with it

Cloning the old SSD cost me in the long run

It seems like an oversight now, but back then, I didn't really recall the occasional Windows corruption that I had experienced on my SATA SSD. Whenever my Windows 10 installation failed to boot, I ran an SFC or DISM scan to fix it. The PC sprang back to life, and I forgot about the corruption until the next time it happened. It was rare enough that I never considered cloning the system partition would create a lasting problem.

The Windows corruption errors started appearing more frequently — it was either a black screen or a boot loop every few months. Instead of attacking the core of the problem, I started making regular system images with Macrium Reflect, so I could revert to a working state if (or when) the system went kaput again.

Even the strange Bluetooth, Sleep, and internet issues that left me stumped didn't convince me that I needed a Windows reinstall. It was only a few months ago when I finally moved to Windows 11 that those problems finally disappeared, along with the frequent system corruption errors.

I finally updated my BIOS — don't wait as long as I did

BIOS updates are nothing to be afraid of; you'd only gain something most of the time

7
By  Tanveer Singh

There's a reason a fresh start is recommended

You don't need to carry over the bloat

After living with an unstable system for years, I finally realized the importance of a clean installation. It wipes almost all the underlying errors of the previous OS installation, wiping the slate clean. Of course, deeper firmware-level corruption or malware will persist, but those are rare. Installing Windows from scratch would have taken me more time and friction, but it would have been better overall.

Starting fresh also removes the system bloat that your PC has accumulated over the years. You don't really need to carry over every single app, setting, and customization to your new SSD. Installing a new copy of Windows allows you to reconsider some choices and gives you an arguably more performant system.

Besides, if there's anything you really want from your old drive, you can always copy those files over after setting up your new SSD. Except for potentially corrupted system files, you can safely copy the data from other partitions once you're satisfied that it's clean. A malware scan will usually do the trick.

Windows 11 feels heavier than it should, and these defaults are part of the problem

For all it does right, Windows 11 could stand to lose plenty of weight

7
By  Samarveer Singh

A clean installation isn't always necessary, but a broken OS demands it

Of course, many users won't have the same experience with cloning their old SSD to a new one. If their Windows copy never really ran into serious problems, chances are that it will work just fine on their new system. When you've faced system instability and corruption, however, it makes sense to jettison the old OS installation. A fresh start minimizes the potential for things going wrong again.

There's a reason a fresh start is recommended

You don't need to carry over the bloat

After living with an unstable system for years, I finally realized the importance of a clean installation. It wipes almost all the underlying errors of the previous OS installation, wiping the slate clean. Of course, deeper firmware-level corruption or malware will persist, but those are rare. Installing Windows from scratch would have taken me more time and friction, but it would have been better overall.

Starting fresh also removes the system bloat that your PC has accumulated over the years. You don't really need to carry over every single app, setting, and customization to your new SSD. Installing a new copy of Windows allows you to reconsider some choices and gives you an arguably more performant system.

Besides, if there's anything you really want from your old drive, you can always copy those files over after setting up your new SSD. Except for potentially corrupted system files, you can safely copy the data from other partitions once you're satisfied that it's clean. A malware scan will usually do the trick.

When you've faced system instability and corruption, however, it makes sense to jettison the old OS installation. A fresh start minimizes the potential for things going wrong again.
